strengths: The paper targets an important and practical CAD problem: using native B-rep inputs rather than only images, point clouds, or natural-language descriptions. This is well motivated for industrial CAD workflows.

The unified MLLM framing across reverse engineering, completion, error correction, and CAD-QA is valuable. Even if many components are adapted from prior work, putting B-rep geometry, Python-like CAD code, and instruction-style task prompts into one framework is a useful direction for general-purpose CAD agents.

The reverse-engineering results on DeepCAD are promising: BrepCoder substantially improves median Chamfer Distance and invalid ratio over reported baselines, while maintaining competitive command and parameter accuracy.
The paper recognizes the non-uniqueness of CAD construction sequences and provides qualitative and statistical analysis showing why command-level accuracy may undervalue geometrically valid outputs.
Ablations cover several relevant design choices, including CoCa-style alignment, freezing the B-rep encoder, LLM scale, projector depth, and the effect of Stage 1 pretraining.
weaknesses: The downstream comparisons are not fully convincing. For completion, CAD-Llama receives text annotations while BrepCoder receives the target B-rep, so the gain partly reflects a much richer input modality rather than the proposed training strategy. For error correction, ReCAD is evaluated across a different dataset and CAD syntax, and GPT/Gemini use rendered images rather than B-reps, making the comparisons only weakly controlled.

The evidence for the claimed two-stage training benefit is mixed. Stage 1 improves CAD-QA substantially, but completion gains are negligible, and error correction has mixed metrics with the No Stage 1 variant sometimes better. This weakens the central claim that reverse-engineering pretraining consistently drives downstream improvements.

The method is largely a composition of existing pieces: UV-Net-style B-rep encoding, CoCa-style alignment, a projector, Qwen, and CAD-Llama-like code representation. The integration is useful, but the algorithmic novelty is moderate and should be positioned more carefully.

Several implementation details needed for reproducibility are missing or underspecified, including training schedules, optimizer settings, batch sizes, decoding strategy, parameter tolerance delta, corruption/noise distributions for error correction, exact prompt templates, and whether code/model weights will be released.

The completion and error-correction tasks use the complete target B-rep as input, which may make them closer to constrained reverse engineering than realistic code completion or debugging from partial/erroneous programs. The paper should clarify the intended use case and avoid overclaiming practical design-assistance capability.

Some methodological descriptions are confusing, especially around the Phase 1 decoder/query formulation and how aligned features are transferred to Stage 1. It is not fully clear whether the exact features optimized by CoCa are the same features consumed by the LLM projector.

The CAD-QA result is competitive but not state-of-the-art, and the comparison to point-cloud MLLMs does not isolate whether B-rep is superior for reasoning; a B-rep-specific or modality-controlled baseline would strengthen the claim.

The paper gives limited discussion of dataset scope and generalization beyond DeepCAD-style synthetic/parametric examples. Industrial B-rep models can be far more complex, and robustness to real CAD kernels, larger assemblies, and varied construction histories is not evaluated.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored CAD/CV problem: using industry-standard B-rep inputs for multiple CAD reasoning tasks rather than relying only on point clouds, images, or task-specific models.
The overall system idea is sensible: align B-rep features with Python-like CAD code, then use an LLM backbone for reverse engineering, completion, error correction, and CAD-QA.
The paper reports results across several tasks and includes ablations for alignment type, encoder freezing, model size, projector depth, and Stage-1 pretraining.
weaknesses: The main novelty is limited. BrepCoder largely combines existing components: UV-Net-style B-rep encoding, CoCa-style alignment, CAD-Llama-style Python-like code, and a Qwen LLM. The paper does not make a convincing case that the technical contribution is more than a system assembly.

The experimental comparisons are often not well controlled. For completion, CAD-Llama receives text annotations while BrepCoder receives B-rep features, so the comparison mixes model quality with input-modality advantage. For error correction, GPT/Gemini receive a single rendered image, ReCAD uses a different syntax and dataset, and BrepCoder receives B-rep, making the large gains hard to interpret as algorithmic progress.

The claimed importance of the two-stage training strategy is weakly supported. Table 3(b) shows almost no improvement for completion, mixed results for error correction, and a clear improvement mainly for CAD-QA. This does not justify the broad claim that Stage 1 generally enables downstream CAD reasoning.

Reverse engineering results are mixed: BrepCoder improves Chamfer Distance and parameter accuracy but is worse than CADCL on command accuracy. The ambiguity discussion is plausible, but the paper does not provide a rigorous equivalence-aware metric or enough analysis to fully support the interpretation.

The evaluation is narrow and mostly synthetic. DeepCAD and SGP-Bench do not demonstrate robustness on real industrial B-reps, complex feature histories, out-of-distribution topology, multi-step assemblies, or noisy imported CAD models. This limits the practical impact of the claimed general-purpose CAD agent.

Important reproducibility details are missing or under-specified, including training schedules, data preprocessing, tokenization/code conversion details, hyperparameters beyond a few architectural choices, prompt formats, decoding settings, and exact construction of corrupted/error-correction examples.

Some reported numbers raise questions. The invalid-ratio scale appears inconsistent across tables, and the dramatic drop from prior methods to 0.009 is not sufficiently explained. The paper should clarify whether IR is a percentage or fraction and how executability is measured.

The CAD-QA result is not state of the art: BrepCoder reaches 79%, below PointLLM at 81%, despite the paper framing this as evidence for broad CAD reasoning. The smaller model size is a useful observation, but not enough to support strong claims.

The manuscript lacks a meaningful limitations discussion. Failure modes such as non-unique design histories, dependence on DeepCAD-style programs, cross-kernel compatibility, scaling to real B-rep complexity, and exact numerical parameter recovery should be treated centrally.

Overall, the topic is worthwhile, but the paper currently overclaims relative to its novelty and evidence. The methodological contribution and experimental rigor are not strong enough for ECCV acceptance in the current form.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: moving CAD learning beyond task-specific models toward a unified B-rep-conditioned MLLM. The motivation is compelling because B-rep is the native industrial representation and many prior CAD MLLM works rely on images, point clouds, text captions, or isolated task architectures.

The proposed formulation is coherent. Converting CAD sequences into Python-like code is a sensible way to exploit code-oriented LLM priors, and the two-stage training pipeline, first learning B-rep-to-code reverse engineering and then adapting to completion, correction, and QA, is well aligned with the stated goal of learning design logic.

Empirical results are encouraging across several tasks. On DeepCAD reverse engineering, BrepCoder substantially improves median Chamfer Distance and invalid ratio over reported baselines while remaining competitive on command and parameter accuracy. The downstream completion and error-correction results are also strong, especially the large gains in parameter accuracy and geometric validity.

The paper provides useful ablations for alignment strategy, encoder freezing, model size, projector depth, and the role of Stage 1 training. The analysis of modeling ambiguity is a valuable discussion because exact command-sequence accuracy can underestimate geometrically correct CAD reconstructions.
The manuscript is generally clear and easy to follow, with a logical progression from representation choice to multimodal alignment, LLM integration, and task-specific evaluation.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat incremental. The system combines established components, including UV-Net-style B-rep encoding, CoCa-style alignment, a projector, and a Qwen backbone. The main contribution is the integration and task unification rather than a fundamentally new modeling mechanism, which slightly limits the originality claim.

Several comparisons are not fully controlled. Completion compares B-rep-conditioned BrepCoder against text-conditioned CAD-Llama, and error correction compares against image-based commercial MLLMs and ReCAD on a different syntax/dataset. These comparisons support the usefulness of B-rep inputs, but they do not cleanly isolate the benefit of the proposed architecture or training strategy.

The evidence for Stage 1 pretraining is mixed for some downstream tasks. Completion gains are very small, and error-correction command accuracy and invalid ratio slightly worsen relative to the no-Stage-1 variant, while the main clear gain is on CAD-QA. The paper would be stronger with deeper analysis of when Stage 1 helps and why.

Experimental details are under-specified for reproducibility. Important information such as optimization settings, training schedules, prompt formats, tokenization details, hardware, decoding strategy, parameter tolerance delta, and dataset construction specifics for corrupted-code generation are either missing or too brief.

The evaluation remains largely within synthetic or benchmark settings derived from DeepCAD and a small CAD-QA benchmark. The claim of general-purpose industrial CAD agency would be better supported by cross-dataset generalization, real-world B-rep models, more complex assemblies, or robustness tests under distribution shift.

The CAD-QA result is competitive but not state-of-the-art, and the comparison to point-cloud MLLMs is hard to interpret because modalities and pretraining histories differ. This is acceptable for a unified framework paper, but it weakens the case for broad visual/geometric reasoning superiority.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful and timely CAD understanding problem: using native B-rep inputs with an LLM-style model for multiple tasks rather than training separate task-specific architectures. This is practically relevant because B-rep is closer to industrial CAD data than point clouds or rendered images.

The overall framework is coherent: Python-like CAD code provides a natural target for an LLM, UV-Net supplies B-rep features, CoCa-style contrastive plus captioning alignment is a sensible pretraining objective, and the two-stage training design is technically plausible.

The reverse engineering results are strong on the reported metrics: BrepCoder substantially improves median Chamfer Distance and invalid ratio over CADCL, DeepCAD, and Brep2Seq, while remaining competitive on command and parameter accuracy.

The paper evaluates several downstream tasks, including completion, error correction, and CAD-QA, and includes ablations over alignment, encoder choice, CLIP vs CoCa alignment, encoder freezing, LLM scale, and projector depth. These ablations support several major design choices.

The discussion of command-sequence ambiguity is useful. The authors correctly note that low command accuracy can coexist with geometrically valid outputs because CAD construction histories are not unique.
weaknesses: The originality is moderate rather than high. Many ingredients are borrowed directly from existing work: CAD-Llama-style Python-like code, UV-Net B-rep encoding, CoCa-style alignment, and Qwen-based multimodal integration. The main contribution is a useful combination and adaptation rather than a clearly new modeling principle.

The downstream evidence is less convincing than the headline suggests. In the Stage 1 ablation, completion barely changes with pretraining, and error correction command accuracy is slightly worse; the strongest gain is CAD-QA. This weakens the claim that reverse-engineering pretraining broadly transfers design logic to all downstream tasks.

Several comparisons are not fully fair or decisive. CAD-Llama receives text annotations rather than B-rep geometry for completion; GPT/Gemini receive a single rendered image for error correction; ReCAD is only compared indirectly across different datasets; and the CAD-QA comparison is against point-cloud MLLMs with different model sizes and pretraining. These baselines are informative but do not isolate the benefit of the proposed architecture cleanly.

The evaluation is largely confined to synthetic or curated benchmarks derived from DeepCAD and SGP-Bench. The paper does not demonstrate robustness on real industrial B-rep files, noisy CAD histories, larger assemblies, non-extrusion-heavy models, or out-of-distribution CAD programs, which limits the strength of the general-purpose CAD-agent claim.

The error-correction setup uses synthetic perturbations such as command permutations and parameter noise, but it is unclear how representative these are of real CAD modeling mistakes. A real-error benchmark or user-study-style evaluation would make this task much more convincing.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for an ECCV-level systems paper. The manuscript gives training hyperparameters but does not clearly state whether code, processed data, prompts, generated corruptions, baseline retraining recipes, or GPT-5 VLM evaluation prompts will be released. GPT-5-based visual scoring is also hard to reproduce and may change over time.

Some claims are overstated. The paper repeatedly frames the model as a general-purpose CAD agent, but it is trained and tested on a narrow set of CAD sequence distributions and multiple-choice QA. The evidence supports a promising B-rep-conditioned CAD code model, not yet a broadly general CAD reasoning agent.

The paper lacks a meaningful limitations and societal-impact discussion. For CAD automation, issues such as invalid designs, manufacturability, intellectual property, safety-critical engineering use, and over-reliance on generated CAD programs are worth addressing.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored CAD setting: direct reasoning over B-rep inputs rather than images or point clouds. A unified model for reverse engineering, completion, error correction, and CAD-QA would be practically valuable if convincingly demonstrated.

The use of Python-like CAD code is sensible and leverages the strengths of code LLMs. The reported invalid-ratio improvements are notable, suggesting that the representation may help produce executable CAD programs.
The manuscript includes several relevant baselines, ablations, and qualitative examples, and the reverse-engineering results show competitive Chamfer Distance and parameter accuracy on DeepCAD.
weaknesses: The core contribution is largely an assembly of existing components: UV-Net-style B-rep encoding, CoCa-style contrastive/captioning alignment, a projector, and Qwen/CAD-Llama-like code generation. The paper does not make a strong case that there is a novel algorithmic idea beyond combining these pieces for CAD.

The downstream task setup is concerning. For completion and error correction, the model receives the target B-rep, which already contains the full geometry. This makes the tasks close to reverse engineering plus conditioning on partial/noisy code, rather than realistic code completion or repair from incomplete information. The claims about engineering reasoning are therefore overstated.

Several baselines are not fairly matched. CAD-Llama receives text annotations rather than B-rep geometry, GPT/Gemini receive only a single rendered image for error correction, and ReCAD is acknowledged as using a different dataset. These comparisons favor BrepCoder and weaken the empirical case.

The central two-stage training claim is weakly supported. In Table 3(b), removing Stage 1 gives nearly identical completion performance and even higher error-correction ACCcmd; only CAD-QA shows a large gain, but that evaluation is small. This undermines the claim that reverse-engineering pretraining is broadly responsible for downstream improvements.

The CAD-QA result is not strong: BrepCoder reaches 79% on a 1K-model multiple-choice benchmark and is below PointLLM, despite the paper presenting it as evidence of general CAD reasoning. The test size, question distribution, and statistical uncertainty are not discussed.

Evaluation metrics have limitations that are not adequately handled. Median Chamfer Distance can hide failure cases; ACCcmd is sensitive to non-unique CAD programs; and the GPT-5 VLM score is not reproducible without prompts, sampling details, or access assumptions.

Reproducibility is insufficient. Important details are missing or vague, including exact data generation for completion/error correction, parameter-noise distributions, baseline retraining recipes, decoding settings, prompts, random seeds, and statistical variance.

The method description has ambiguities. The role of Phase 1 alignment in Phase 2 is not fully convincing, since the LLM projector uses encoder features rather than the CoCa generation features, and some equations/descriptions of decoder queries and captioning loss are unclear.

The experimental scope is narrow: most results are on synthetic DeepCAD-derived data, with little evidence of generalization to real industrial B-reps, out-of-distribution CAD complexity, or more realistic corrupted/incomplete design histories.

The paper’s claims are stronger than the evidence. It repeatedly frames the model as a general-purpose CAD agent with high-level engineering reasoning, but the experiments mostly show supervised reconstruction on aligned synthetic data under favorable input conditions.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically meaningful problem: using industry-standard B-rep inputs rather than only point clouds/images for multi-task CAD reasoning. The framing of B-rep-to-Python-like CAD code as a bridge to LLM reasoning is well motivated.

BrepCoder is a coherent unified framework covering reverse engineering, completion, error correction, and CAD-QA with one MLLM-style architecture. This is a valuable step beyond narrowly task-specific CAD models.

The empirical results are strong on the core CAD-code tasks. On reverse engineering, the method substantially improves Chamfer Distance and invalid ratio over prior B-rep baselines while maintaining competitive command/parameter accuracy. Completion and error correction also show clear gains over retrained B-rep baselines.

The paper includes useful ablations for multimodal alignment, encoder choice, CoCa versus CLIP-style alignment, freezing, LLM scale/backbone, projector depth, and Stage 1 pretraining. These ablations generally support the proposed design choices.

The discussion of modeling ambiguity is thoughtful. The authors correctly note that command-level matching can penalize geometrically valid alternative CAD programs, and they provide qualitative and statistical evidence to contextualize the slightly lower command accuracy.

The method appears reasonably reproducible at the algorithmic level: architecture choices, training stages, optimizer settings, batch sizes, hardware, and datasets are described in both the main paper and supplement.
weaknesses: The evidence for broad general-purpose CAD reasoning is still somewhat limited. Most CAD-code experiments rely on DeepCAD-derived data and synthetic perturbations/masking, so it is unclear how well the method transfers to real industrial B-reps, more complex assemblies, richer feature operations, or out-of-distribution design conventions.

The downstream benefit of Stage 1 pretraining is mixed for completion and error correction: gains are very small for completion, and error-correction command accuracy is actually slightly higher without Stage 1. The strongest Stage 1 effect is CAD-QA, so the claim that reverse-engineering pretraining broadly drives downstream CAD-code performance should be stated more cautiously.

Some baselines are not perfectly comparable. CAD-Llama receives textual annotations rather than B-rep geometry, and GPT/Gemini are evaluated from rendered 2D images because they cannot consume B-reps. These comparisons are informative but do not fully isolate the advantage of the proposed architecture against equally privileged multimodal baselines.

The CAD-QA evaluation is relatively modest: SGP-Bench has only 1K models, and BrepCoder is competitive but not best-performing against PointLLM. This supports transferability but is weaker evidence for superior general CAD semantic reasoning.

The VLM-based visual quality metric using GPT-5 is potentially hard to reproduce and may introduce evaluator bias. It is useful as a supplemental signal, but the paper should not lean heavily on it without more details on prompts, sampling, variance, and consistency checks.

The paper does not sufficiently discuss limitations and failure modes beyond modeling ambiguity. Important issues such as invalid generated code patterns, sensitivity to B-rep complexity, topological degeneracies, longer sequences, CAD kernel execution errors, and real-world deployment constraints deserve more explicit analysis.
